name: Private State Tokens
plain: Anonymous tokens that carry a trust signal across sites without identifying the person.
meaning: An issuer vouches that a visitor looks human and later redeemers read that single bit, unlinked to identity. Chrome lists it as Continue to support after Oct 2025. Issuer limit: 2 issuers per origin used per top frame (soft cap).

access.persistence: Tokens expire per issuer; limited batch per issuer
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

safari.note: Safari has separate Private Access Tokens (iOS 16)

limits.headline: Can carry a trust signal between sites without telling them who you are
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a site checks if you are a real person
can: Hold a token that says you were judged real by a first site
Show the token to a second site to prove it
Keep the two sites from linking the visits
cannot: Tell the second site who you are
Work in Firefox or Safari, and only in tests on iPhone browsers
Last forever; tokens run out and are limited in number
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge support it. Safari on iPhone is partial. Firefox does not support it.

story.what_it_is: Anonymous tokens that carry a trust signal across sites without naming you.

marketing.name: Private State Tokens
marketing.pitch: Chrome says the tokens let a site share a trust signal, such as this visitor seems human, without cross site tracking.

story.for_you: You never see it. A site you trust can vouch that you look like a real person, in a token. Another site can read that single bit and let you through without a puzzle.
story.for_makers: Fraud and bot teams want a clue about a visitor when they have no history with them. The token passes a yes or no without a name. It helps cut CAPTCHA puzzles for real people.

use_cases.example: A new visitor to a ticket site shows a token from a trusted site, so the site skips a CAPTCHA.
An ad network reads a token to decide if a click is from a real person, before it bills the advertiser.
A game site lets you skip the bot puzzle at sign up, because a token shows you are human.
A checkout page uses a token as one fraud signal for a new customer.
A social site rate limits fake sign ups by asking for a human token.
A news site shows a sign up wall only to visitors without a human token.

risks: Issuers hold power over who is trusted
Few sites use it so far

abuse: Gatekeeping content on opaque trust score
